title: Diabetes: what it is and common warning signs
text: Diabetes is a condition where blood sugar stays too high because the body does not make enough insulin or cannot use it well. Common warning signs include increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, tiredness, blurred vision and slow-healing wounds. Type 2 diabetes is strongly linked with excess weight, inactivity and family history. Diagnosis needs a blood test (fasting glucose, HbA1c or an oral glucose tolerance test) ordered by a doctor.

title: Lowering diabetes risk
text: Regular physical activity (about 150 minutes of brisk walking per week), keeping a healthy weight, eating more vegetables, whole grains and pulses, and cutting sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates all lower type 2 diabetes risk. People with a family history, high blood pressure or past gestational diabetes should get blood sugar checked regularly.

title: Heart disease risk factors
text: Major risk factors for heart disease are high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, heavy alcohol use and family history. Not smoking, regular exercise, a diet low in salt and saturated fat, and controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar greatly reduce risk.

title: Heart attack warning signs
text: Warning signs of a heart attack: chest pressure, tightness or pain lasting more than a few minutes, pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck or back, shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea or light-headedness. Women may have less typical symptoms such as unusual fatigue, nausea or back/jaw pain. This is an emergency: call the ambulance number immediately, keep the person resting, and do not let them drive themselves.

title: Stroke: recognise FAST
text: FAST: Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness or numbness, Speech slurred or confused, Time to call emergency services immediately. Other signs include sudden severe headache, sudden vision loss and sudden loss of balance. Note the time symptoms began because treatment is time-critical. Do not give food, drink or medicines.

title: Parkinson's disease overview
text: Parkinson's disease is a progressive nervous-system disorder. Typical early signs are a resting tremor, slowness of movement, muscle stiffness, smaller handwriting, a softer voice and reduced facial expression. Voice measurements such as jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio are research markers used by screening models, but diagnosis is made by a neurologist from clinical examination. Treatment can help control symptoms.

title: High blood pressure
text: Blood pressure is classified as normal below 120/80 mm Hg, elevated at 120-129 systolic with diastolic under 80, stage 1 hypertension at 130-139 or 80-89, stage 2 at 140/90 or above, and a hypertensive crisis above 180/120 which needs urgent medical care if accompanied by chest pain, breathlessness, confusion or severe headache. Reducing salt, exercising, limiting alcohol, not smoking and taking prescribed medication regularly help control it.

title: Who can donate blood
text: In general a blood donor should be healthy, aged 18 to 65, weigh at least 50 kg, have haemoglobin of at least 12.5 g/dL, and feel well on the day. Whole-blood donations should be spaced at least 3 months apart (many guidelines allow 56-90 days depending on country and sex). People with fever, recent infection, recent tattoos or piercings, pregnancy, breastfeeding, certain chronic diseases or some medications may need to wait or be deferred. The blood bank's doctor makes the final decision.

title: Blood group compatibility
text: O negative red cells can be given to any patient (universal red-cell donor). AB positive patients can receive red cells from any group (universal recipient). O positive can donate to all positive groups; A negative can donate to A and AB groups; for plasma the pattern is reversed, AB plasma is universal. Hospitals always cross-match blood before transfusion.

title: After donating blood
text: After donating, drink extra fluids, avoid heavy exercise and alcohol for the rest of the day, keep the bandage on for several hours, eat a normal balanced meal, and lie down if you feel dizzy. Iron-rich foods such as leafy greens, pulses, meat and fortified cereals help the body recover.

title: First aid: severe bleeding
text: Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or bandage and keep pressing without lifting to check. Raise the injured limb if possible. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top rather than removing it. Call the ambulance number for heavy bleeding, and keep the person lying down and warm. Use a tourniquet only if trained and bleeding in a limb cannot be controlled.

title: First aid: burns
text: Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes, remove rings and tight items near the burn before swelling, and cover loosely with clean non-fluffy material such as cling film. Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste or burst blisters. Seek emergency care for burns larger than the person's palm, on the face, hands, genitals or joints, electrical or chemical burns, and any burn in a child or older adult.

title: First aid: choking adult
text: If the person cannot cough, speak or breathe, give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre). Alternate until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive, then call emergency services and begin CPR. For infants use back blows and chest thrusts only, never abdominal thrusts.

title: CPR for an unresponsive adult not breathing normally
text: Call the ambulance number or ask someone else to. Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about 5-6 cm deep at 100-120 compressions per minute, letting the chest rise fully between pushes. If trained, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions. Use an automated external defibrillator (AED) as soon as one is available and follow its voice prompts. Continue until help arrives.

title: Fever care
text: For adults a temperature of 38 C (100.4 F) or above is a fever. Rest, drink plenty of fluids and use paracetamol according to the label. Seek medical care for fever lasting over 3 days, a temperature above 39.5 C, stiff neck, severe headache, rash, confusion, breathing difficulty, or any fever in a baby under 3 months.

title: Dehydration and oral rehydration
text: Signs of dehydration include thirst, dark urine, dry mouth, dizziness and tiredness. For diarrhoea or vomiting give oral rehydration solution (ORS) in small frequent sips. Seek medical help if the person cannot keep fluids down, is very drowsy, has no urine for 8 hours, or is an infant or elderly.

title: Everyday habits that protect health
text: Aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, 7-9 hours of sleep, plenty of fruit, vegetables and whole grains, limited salt, sugar and ultra-processed food, no tobacco, limited alcohol, regular health check-ups, and managing stress. Adults over 30 should periodically check blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol.

title: Mental wellbeing support
text: Persistent sadness, anxiety, loss of interest or sleep changes lasting more than two weeks are worth discussing with a doctor or counsellor. If someone is thinking of harming themselves, encourage them to contact local emergency services or a crisis helpline right away and not to stay alone.

title: First aid: seizure
text: Stay calm, note the time, clear hard objects away, cushion the head, do not restrain the person or put anything in their mouth. Once shaking stops, roll them onto their side (recovery position). Call emergency services if it lasts over 5 minutes, repeats, the person is injured, pregnant, has diabetes, or does not wake up normally.

title: About this platform's AI models
text: The diagnosis module uses machine-learning models (logistic regression, SVM, random forest and a feed-forward neural network were compared; the best by cross-validation is used) trained on public datasets: Pima Indians diabetes, Cleveland heart disease and Oxford Parkinson's voice data. They are small datasets, so results are screening estimates only and never a diagnosis.
